title: Pope Says Sorry for Church's Part in Slavery — A First in History!
summary: For the first time ever, a pope has apologized for the Vatican's part in making slavery legal long ago. On Monday, Pope Leo XIV said he was deeply sorry that past popes gave European kings permission to capture and enslave people, especially in Africa and the Americas. In a special letter called an encyclical, he called this a 'wound in Christian memory.' Back in the 1400s, popes wrote official documents that let Portugal and Spain conquer lands and force non-Christians into slavery. One document from 1452 even said the Portuguese could 'reduce their persons to perpetual slavery.' The pope said it's not fair to judge people from the past by today's standards, but the Church waited too long to say slavery was wrong. Pope Leo is the first U.S.-born pope, and his own family history includes both enslaved people and slave owners. A historian named Shannen Dee Williams said Black Catholics have waited a long time for this apology and called it a 'monumental step.' The pope's letter also talks about new kinds of slavery today, like how technology can control people.
why_it_matters: This teaches us that it's never too late to say sorry for past mistakes, and that treating everyone equally is an important value in our communities.

background_read: Pope Leo XIV is the first pope from the United States. He leads the Catholic Church from the Vatican, a tiny independent country inside Rome, Italy.
In the 1400s, popes had the power to tell European kings to capture new lands and even allowed slavery.
The Catholic Church is one of the world's largest religions, with over a billion followers.
Article_Structure: WHO: Pope Leo XIV, past popes, historian Shannen Dee Williams, and Black Catholics.
WHAT: The Pope issued an apology for the Catholic Church's historical role in legalizing slavery, calling it a wound in Christian memory.
WHERE: From the Vatican, the headquarters of the Catholic Church.
WHY: To acknowledge the Church's past wrongs and address the long wait for such an apology from Black Catholics.

perspectives.description: Black Catholics and many others see this apology as a long-awaited step toward recognizing past injustices and healing wounds.
Some people feel that words aren't enough, and that the Church should do more to address the lasting effects of slavery.
Historians note that this is the first time a pope has officially apologized, marking an important moment in Catholic Church history.
